### Observed differences

- All six activities that carry resource assignments show the same reallocation of work. In the earlier window, each activity was handled mainly by one stable group of resources, led by User_49 with roughly 8–11 assignments in 100 per activity; in the later window, that group has fallen out of the leading assignees and a largely different group, led by User_3 with about 8–9 in 100, carries the same activities. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- Work also became more dispersed: the share of assignments going to resources outside the ten most-used rose from about 28–44 in 100 per activity in the earlier window to about 39–51 in 100 in the later window. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- One resource, User_51, is the exception, keeping a similar share in both windows (about 4–8 assignments in 100 per activity). [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- Each profile difference is about 0.39–0.49 on its own scale and exceeds about 1995 of 2000 random re-splits of the pooled windows; the profiles rest on 134–271 assignment observations per window (200 traces per window). [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- For context, the resource family produced 6 qualifying items where about 0.004 would be expected if nothing had changed, while the control-flow family (0 of 33 units) and the timing family (0 of 35 units) produced no items at all. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a change in resource allocation as a possibility: for A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22, the work appears to have moved from one group of resources (previously led by User_49) to a largely different group (now led by User_3), with assignments also spread across somewhat more distinct resources in the later window. This rests on all six assignment profiles shifting in the same direction with the same resources leaving and entering the leading ranks, each difference being larger than about 1995 of 2000 random re-splits, the resource family yielding 6 items against roughly 0.004 expected without change while no control-flow or timing items appeared, and every profile being backed by 134–271 observations per window. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

Limitations: the six items most likely describe one underlying reallocation rather than six independent changes, and the resource codes are anonymous, so the evidence shows only that the distribution of assignments changed, not why or whether the incoming resources were already active at smaller shares before. An important competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is that the later window simply contains a different mix of cases that happens to be handled by different resources, rather than a change in how work is assigned. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
